papers.title: Genetic control and tissue specificity of transcriptomic rhythmicity
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms influence molecular traits in most tissues, yet genetic studies mostly treat molecular measurements as static. In particular, genetic effects on gene expression are typically investigated through expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) studies, which ignore sampling time and therefore miss genetic effects on rhythm parameters such as amplitude and acrophase. In this study, we used a cosinor-based joint genotype-by-rhythm interaction framework applied to GTEx version 10 gene expression data, with donor inferred phase as a proxy for circadian time. We first identified rhythmically expressed genes in 49 of the 50 tissues profiled in GTEx. We then tested common variants within 50 kb of each rhythmic gene's transcription start site for genetic regulation of transcriptomic rhythmicity. We identified 167 circadian expression QTLs (cd-eQTLs), comprising 54 lead signals for 51 genes across 28 tissues. Most cd-eQTLs altered oscillation amplitude, while others affected acrophase or both. We then investigated the tissue specificity of cd-eQTLs and found that those acting on core circadian genes had consistent effects across tissues, whereas those acting on clock-regulated genes were largely tissue-specific. A phenome-wide association study in the Pan-UK Biobank linked 34 cd-eQTLs to 100 phenotypes, including self-reported chronotype, adiposity, blood cell counts and blood biochemistry. These results show that genetic variation shapes circadian gene expression in a tissue-dependent manner, and that accounting for time of day reveals regulatory effects that static eQTL analyses cannot detect.

papers.title: 14-3-3 Enables β-Adrenergic Regulation of the Cardiac Sodium Channel at the Intercalated Disc
papers.abstract: Background: Beta-Adrenergic stimulation enables the heart to adapt electrical activity to increased physiological demand. Although the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 is essential for impulse propagation, the mechanisms underlying its acute beta-adrenergic regulation, particularly within distinct cardiomyocyte membrane domains, remain poorly understood. We investigated whether the phosphorylation-sensitive adaptor protein 14-3-3 mediates this regulation. Methods and Results: Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs), we found that isoproterenol rapidly increased sodium current (INa) and promoted channel activation at more hyperpolarized potentials, whereas PKA inhibition reduced INa. Disruption of 14-3-3 function abolished these responses without substantially altering basal sodium current or Nav1.5 surface expression. Macropatch recordings from ventricular myocytes revealed that isoproterenol preferentially enhanced INa at the intercalated disc, an effect prevented by 14-3-3 inhibition. Proximity ligation assays further demonstrated increased Nav1.5/14-3-3 proximity following beta-adrenergic stimulation. Systematic mutagenesis identified S460 in the Nav1.5 DI-DII linker as a critical determinant of acute PKA-dependent regulation. Molecular modeling predicted that S460 phosphorylation stabilizes the Nav1.5/14-3-3 interaction. In CRISPR-engineered S460A iPSC-CMs, acute beta-adrenergic regulation of INa was abolished, whereas the isoproterenol-induced increase in conduction velocity was significantly attenuated. Computational simulations further predicted that enhanced intercalated-disc sodium current supports increased conduction velocity across varying conditions of electrical coupling and pacing rate. Conclusions: Our findings identify 14-3-3 and S460 as critical determinants of spatially selective beta-adrenergic regulation of Nav1.5 at the cardiac intercalated disc. This mechanism provides a molecular link between sympathetic signaling and cardiac sodium current regulation, supporting the concept that localized enhancement of Nav1.5 function contributes to the adaptation of cardiac conduction during increased sympathetic demand.

papers.title: Characterising sleep spindle emergence in infancy: Effects of prematurity and early locomotor intervention
papers.abstract: Study objectives: Sleep spindles are thalamocortical oscillations evolving during early brain maturation. In adults, they support memory consolidation and are organised into rhythmic "trains" thought to support memory reactivation. How this temporal organisation emerges in infancy, and whether prematurity or early sensorimotor experience shapes it, remains unclear. This study characterised infant spindles and investigated how prematurity and early locomotor training affect their temporal and spatial organisation, providing insight into early brain maturation. Methods: Daytime high-density EEG sleep recordings were analysed in 50 infants born full-term (n=12) or very preterm (n=38, including 12 who received locomotor training) at 2 months corrected age. Spindle temporal organisation was analysed using a two-step Morlet wavelet transform to quantify slow modulations of spindle-band power (11-16Hz). Time-frequency decomposition around spindle onset was used to identify significant spindle-band scalp-wide activity, and topographical maps were statistically compared between groups. Results: All groups showed rhythmic spindle organisation, three times slower than in adults, with no group differences. Untrained preterm infants showed a more diffuse spindle-band activity than the distinct frontal and central clusters observed in full-term infants. Trained preterm infants exhibited a spatial distribution closely resembling that of full-term infants, although their frontal spindle density was lower than in both other groups. Conclusions: Spindle rhythmic organisation emerged early in infancy and remained unaffected by prematurity or locomotor training. Prematurity was associated with more diffuse spindle-band activity, suggesting reduced cortical specialisation, whereas trained preterm infants showed a spatial distribution resembling that of full-term infants, suggesting that early locomotor experience may influence thalamocortical organisation.

papers.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
papers.abstract: Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

papers.title: Covert attentional tracking with invisible phase tagging
papers.abstract: Attention forms a fundamental component of visual processing. The locus and spread of covert attention reveals how specific locations or features in the environment are preferentially processed, however, tracking this process in a time-resolved fashion is not easy. Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) is a recent advance in localizing covert attention. This technique uses stimuli that flicker at unique frequencies to invisibly "tag" areas of the visual field. The frequency-specific response elicited offers a measure of visual processing (and covert attention) over time. However, the narrow frequency band compatible with RIFT restricts the number of distinct frequency tags that can be simultaneously used. This limitation can be addressed by using oscillatory phase as an additional tagging feature. Here, we conducted a RIFT-EEG experiment (n=24) with 8 unique tags based on both frequency and phase modulation. We show that modulations in visual processing can be measured at several tagged locations with identical frequency but different phases. This also allowed for the use of combined phase- and frequency- modulated RIFT to quantify the distribution of attention across the visual field. By integrating phase-modulation into invisible frequency tagging studies of attention, we bring the field a step closer towards fine-resolution attentional tracking continuously over time and space, allowing novel insights across various domains of visual cognition.

papers.title: Inferring brain structural complexity from dynamical measures
papers.abstract: Complexity, commonly defined as the coexistence of integration and differentiation, is a fundamental property of thalamocortical networks and is regarded as a prerequisite for adaptive brain function and consciousness. A variety of metrics have been developed to estimate neural complexity from recorded activity and are increasingly employed in both research and clinical settings. Yet, the extent to which these measures reflect specific architectural features of the underlying circuits remains poorly understood. Here, we used Wilson-Cowan mean-field equations to simulate neural dynamics across networks spanning a broad range of architectures. By systematically rewiring connectivity, we generated graded variations in the structural integration-differentiation balance and assessed a panel of complexity measures derived either from spontaneous activity (observational metrics) or from responses to external perturbations (perturbational metrics). Observational measures exhibited markedly heterogeneous behavior: some were primarily sensitive to network integration, others to differentiation, whereas some showed limited sensitivity to architectural manipulations. In contrast, perturbational measures robustly peaked at intermediate rewiring steps and scaled with small-worldness, consistent with architectures that combine local recurrence and distributed communication. Moreover, perturbational metrics proved robust to common-driver confounds and were highest in a wake-like regime near critical instability, declining as sleep-like dynamics became more widespread across the network. Taken together, these findings map widely used empirical complexity measures onto specific network architectures, reveal dynamical factors that can bias observational estimates, and provide guidance for inferring complexity in systems whose internal organization is inaccessible, unconventional, or only partially known, including brain organoids, non-human nervous systems, and synthetic neural networks.

papers.title: Characterization of Fetal Cortical Development Using Spectral Analysis of Gyrification (SPANGY)
papers.abstract: The prenatal period of human brain development is critical for mental health and cognition across the entire lifespan. During this period, the cortex undergoes a dramatic transformation from a smooth lissencephalic surface into an elaborately folded structure, a process whose precise characterization is essential for understanding neurodevelopmental trajectories. This study represents the first application of Spectral Analysis of Gyrification (SPANGY) to a large multi-centric fetal brain MRI dataset (635 subjects, 20-38 weeks gestational age). SPANGY characterizes geometric variations on a surface based on the wavelength of folds, hence, providing a quantitative local description of gyrification at the individual level. Using rigorous normative modeling (GAMLSS) and statistical harmonization (ComBat-GAM), we established age-specific reference trajectories for multi-scale gyrification features (spectral frequency bands). We provide the first ever quantification of the temporally-ordered emergence of cortical folding in successive waves during the entire second half of pregnancy: the earliest-emerging low frequency, deep fissures are progressively superseded by the accelerating expansion of higher frequency folds. The normative curves provide the first step in taking prenatal neurodevelopmental assessment from qualitative inspection into a rigorous statistical inference, creating an objective reference against which deviations from healthy brain growth could be caught earlier.

papers.title: Localized Chromatin Rewiring Shapes Rhythmic Transcription within a Stable 3D Genome in Rice
papers.abstract: How spatial genome architecture coordinates rhythmic gene transcription across scales in plants remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated bridge linker Hi-C (BL-Hi-C), H3K9ac ChIP-seq and RNA-seq at six time points across a 24-h circadian cycle in rice. While global higher-order structure was largely invariant, with 84.5% of A/B compartments and over 95% of topologically associating domains (TADs) conserved across all time points, we identified 557 dynamic compartment transitions coupled to changes in active chromatin marks. Within this stable structural scaffold, 35.8% of TADs containing clustered loci of multiple rhythmic genes with synchronized expression phases. In contrast, fine-scale intradomain contacts and chromatin loops exhibited pronounced temporal plasticity. Chromatin interactions connected rhythmic genes with diverse expression phases. Myb-binding motifs were enriched at chromatin interaction anchors at dawn and early day (ZT0 and ZT4). Together, our findings demonstrate that localized chromatin rewiring occurs within relatively stable architectural frameworks, providing a spatiotemporal context for circadian gene regulation in rice.

papers.title: EEG-guided robotic control of transcranial magnetic stimulation
papers.abstract: Brain-state-guided and closed-loop transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) protocols have emerged as methods for decreasing the outcome variability and increasing the therapeutic effectiveness of stimulation protocols. However, existing brain-state-dependent TMS systems control only stimulation timing, while the location is fixed and manually adjusted between blocks or sessions. This limits targeting distributed cortical networks in a flexible brain-state-dependent paradigm. We developed a method that jointly manages TMS pulse timing and location automatically controlled by electroencephalography (EEG)-derived brain state. A machine-learning algorithm infers the brain state in real time to guide robotic coil placement. We present a proof-of-concept study in which EEG controlled both the target site and the timing of TMS. A pre-trained convolutional neural network discriminated between resting state and movements performed with the right or left hand; the classifier output determined the hemisphere in which primary-motor-cortex hand area was stimulated. Preprocessing and decoding of 2-s EEG segments required 150 ms, and the robot took 7.5 s to move from the vertex home position to the predefined motor targets. The EEG-guided robotic TMS method expands the toolkit for brain-state-dependent neurostimulation by enabling closed-loop control of stimulus location based on EEG-derived brain states, including volitional activity. Thus, the method can benefit both neuroscience research and clinical neuromodulation applications, such as by optimizing stimulation parameters to the brain state that produces optimal rehabilitation outcomes in spinal cord injury or motor disorders.

papers.title: Neuroline: an integrated modular pipeline for FAIR multimodal neurophysiology data processing
papers.abstract: The adoption of FAIR principles for code and data sharing in systems neuroscience is hindered by the size and diversity of datasets, the multitude of data formats and the complexity of analysis workflows. These challenges have led to the development of various data standards and modality-specific processing and analysis tools. However, it remains difficult to integrate the diverse processed data streams originating from state-of-the-art neurophysiology experiments into a common format, which is crucial for cross-modal analyses and open, FAIR sharing of data. To address this, we developed Neuroline, a Python package for processing neurophysiology data (electrophysiology, optical imaging, and behaviour) that combines multimodal integration, modularity, and standardised output within a single pipeline. It leverages established packages and consolidates the resulting processed data into the standardised Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) format. Neuroline provides a unified interface while preserving flexibility and extensibility. Here we describe the implementation and challenges of a pipeline capable of integrating different types of neuroscientific data and packages. Finally, we address how Neuroline contributes to the sustainability and accessibility of neuroscience data and software.

papers.title: Metabolic-State-Dependent Magnetic Field Effects on Endogenous Flavin Autofluorescence in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that endogenous autofluorescent molecules in Escherichia coli exhibit fluorescence changes exceeding 10% in response to a 25 mT magnetic field under specific physiological and excitation conditions. Fluorescence spectral analysis strongly supports a flavin origin of the magnetically sensitive signal, with a slight blue shift relative to free flavin suggesting a protein-associated population. The analysis further suggests that this magnetic response originates from a flavin-related component contributing only part of the total cellular autofluorescence. This implies that the magnetic field effect exceeding 10% observed in total cellular autofluorescence represents an ensemble-averaged response, and that the intrinsic magnetic field effect within the magnetically sensitive flavin population may be substantially larger. Notably, the magnetic field effect is strongly suppressed by carbon-source supplementation. These findings indicate that the manifestation of the magnetic field effect is associated with the cellular physiological or metabolic state. The field-induced negative fluorescence response and the saturation of the magnetic-field dependence support the radical-pair mechanism and are consistent with a triplet-born radical-pair reaction. This work provides a framework for identifying endogenous biomolecular candidates exhibiting large intracellular magnetic field effects and suggests a new route toward label-free readout of cellular metabolic states based on flavin magnetosensitivity.

papers.title: Loss of PEA-15 Alters ERK/MAPK Signaling and Circadian Function in the Suprachiasmatic Nucleus
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are a fundamental biological process that coordinates physiological functions, behavior, and metabolism with an approximately 24-hour periodicity. At the center of the mammalian circadian timing system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which generates robust, clock-gated neuronal output that establishes the temporal organization of cellular and physiological processes throughout the body. Our previous work demonstrated that the scaffold protein PEA-15 (phosphoprotein enriched in astrocytes 15) is highly expressed in the SCN and dynamically interacts with ERK, a key effector kinase of the MAPK pathway, to regulate its subcellular localization. Given the important role of ERK/MAPK signaling in circadian timing and photic entrainment, we extended this work using PEA-15 knockout (PEA-15-/-) mice to determine how loss of PEA-15 affects circadian timing, entrainment, and ERK signaling within the SCN. At the cellular level, both clock-gated and light-evoked ERK activation were significantly reduced in PEA-15-/- mice compared with wild-type controls. Under constant darkness, PEA-15-/- mice exhibited a significantly shorter free-running period and reduced locomotor activity relative to wild-type animals. Assessment of circadian entrainment using jet-lag resetting and Aschoff type I light-pulse paradigms revealed a blunted phase-delay response to light and an accelerated rate of entrainment to a phase-advancing light stimulus. Thus, loss of PEA-15 alters multiple properties of the SCN clock, including its intrinsic period and its responsiveness to photic input, with effects that depend on the direction of phase resetting. Collectively, these findings identify PEA-15 as an important regulator of SCN circadian function and implicate ERK/MAPK signaling as one mechanism through which PEA-15 modulates clock timing and photic entrainment.

papers.title: Linking cross-species hemodynamics with neuronal activity in prefrontal cortex during abstract sequence viewing
papers.abstract: The ability to identify and predict abstract sequential patterns enables a wide range of complex cognition and behavior, but the mechanisms mediating it remain poorly understood. Lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) has been implicated in abstract sequence tracking in both humans and macaques, but it is unclear whether underlying processes are shared across species. Furthermore, most existing evidence relies on hemodynamic responses, which can have variable relationships with neuronal activity in a region. We leverage a combination of human fMRI, monkey fMRI, and monkey electrophysiology to bridge these gaps. We find that humans and non-human primates show functionally homologous hemodynamic activation in LPFC during abstract sequence viewing, and neuronal responses within fMRI-targeted regions in macaques contain information about sensory and abstract variables in parallel. However, neuronal activity does not directly mirror hemodynamic responses, and abstract sequence responses are found both near and far from fMRI peaks. In contrast, distinct dynamics of spiking activity are selectively present near fMRI peaks, suggesting that temporal coordination across neurons may influence hemodynamic activity in prefrontal cortex. Together, these experiments establish a link between human brain activity, macaque fMRI, and single neuron responses, providing a window into the neural processes that mediate abstract sequence detection.

papers.title: Habitual sleep duration is associated with the cortical organisation of brain network controllability
papers.abstract: Sleep is fundamental to adaptive brain function, yet how habitual sleep relates to the structural network properties that support flexible transitions between brain states remains poorly understood. Combining wrist-accelerometer sleep measures with diffusion MRI connectomes from 15,799 UK Biobank adults, we show that longer workday sleep is associated with higher modal controllability of somatomotor systems and lower controllability of visual cortex. This system-specific signature reproduced in a locked test set (n = 4,740) and was robust across extensive sensitivity analyses. Decomposition showed that it reflects a redistribution of structural connection weight, with greater absolute visual connectivity and a smaller somatomotor share of the whole-brain total. Weekend catch-up sleep showed no comparable association. The signature was distinct from brain-ageing patterns and, across 1,226 phenotypes, related mainly to physical activity and body composition rather than cognition. These findings link everyday sleep habits to the system-specific organisation of brain network controllability.

papers.title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
papers.abstract: Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. However, how familiarity alters the coordination of neural representations across distributed brain networks remains unclear. Rhythmic neural activity provides a potential mechanism for coordinating information across sensory and higher-order brain regions in the light of previous experience. Here, we thus investigated whether familiarity alters the coordination of brain rhythms during naturalistic viewing. Participants who were either familiar or unfamiliar with the television series Game of Thrones viewed clips from the series while EEG or fMRI was recorded. We calculated the intersubject correlations of neural activity across EEG frequency bands and related this rhythmic activity to fMRI BOLD responses. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

papers.title: How well does electrical source imaging reconstruct neural time series? Evidence from simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings
papers.abstract: Electrical source imaging (ESI) estimates neural activity from scalp EEG, but its ability to reconstruct the temporal dynamics of spontaneous brain activity beyond source localization remains unclear. This is assessed using simultaneous high-density EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings during spontaneous activity in 34 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Four ESI approaches (three distributed source models and one beamformer) are applied to estimate neural activity, which is then projected onto iEEG electrode locations to generate virtual iEEG signals for comparison with measured recordings. Reconstruction fidelity is quantified using Pearson correlations between actual and virtual iEEG signals, while spatial accuracy is assessed through peak localization error and spatial deviation derived from point-spread and cross-talk functions. Analyses are performed in broadband and delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Temporal reconstruction remains limited, with the highest estimated correlation reaching 0.126, localization errors of approximately 3 cm, and substantial spatial leakage. Reconstruction quality decreases with electrode depth and increasing frequency, while improving with higher epileptic spike rates. No single method is optimal across all metrics, although beamforming shows the weakest temporal reconstruction. These findings indicate that ESI only partially captures spontaneous intracranial dynamics and define spatial and temporal constraints for interpreting EEG-based source reconstructions.

papers.title: Roles of Neuromedin-U and Endothelin-1 in human cardiac organoid differentiation
papers.abstract: During recent years, many new culture methods have been established to generate cardiomyocytes, using signaling and patterning factors that play important roles in mammalian heart development. Here, we identify two additional pathways of interest using a cardiac differentiation roadmap that we have generated, involving the endothelin 1 receptor EDNRA gene, and the Neuromedin family signaling peptide gene NMU. Treatment with NMU had most effect in ventricular lineages where it normally is not abundantly expressed, leading to a significant shift from ventricular cardiomyocyte (vCM) differentiation to non-myocytes, as shown with reporters and cell type-specific markers, which was associated with an increased beating frequency. This was not observed in atrial cultures. Treating atrial cultures with endothelin 1 (ET-1, EDN1) increased the number of atrial cardiomyocytes (aCM), while reducing repolarization times, increasing the contraction frequencies and altering the patterns of action potential propagations across the tissue. In ventricular cultures, a reduction in ventricular cardiomyocyte (vCM) numbers was observed, suggesting a combinatorial effect of ET-1 and retinoic acid (RA) on cardiomyocyte differentiation. These results identify ET-1 and NMU as important signaling factors for cardiomyocyte differentiation and electrophysiology of cardiac organoids, with ET-1 enhancing aCM differentiation when added around the time of posteriorization of the second heart field. NMU added without RA reduces the number of vCMs in the culture while it changes the organoids to exhibit a more atrial-like beating frequency.

papers.title: Very Early Cortical Auditory Responses to Speech in Humans
papers.abstract: A foundational measure of the auditory system's ability to process sound correctly is the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and middle latency response (MLR) complex, but their dependence on stimulus complexity and behavioral relevance is poorly understood. Here we recorded noninvasive, simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) in adults listening to both naturalistic speech and clicks, and computed the resulting temporal response functions (TRFs). The TRF's ABR-MLR complex for speech listening contains a very early cortical peak (11 ms latency), which has not been well-characterized, and is absent for click stimuli. Other significant differences in latency and source between the speech and click MLR complexes point to further differences in their auditory processing, in thalamus and cortex. In contrast, the speech and click TRF's ABR complex both share a similar, prominent wave V response. In summation, the use of naturalistic speech reveals how early auditory responses reflect its ethological relevance.

papers.title: Scalp EEG detects motor sequence replay signatures during wakeful rest
papers.abstract: Brief wakeful rest may support motor-memory processing through replay of recently practiced neural sequences, but human motor replay has been demonstrated mainly with invasive recordings or magnetoencephalography. Here we tested whether ordered motor-sequence replay can be detected from scalp EEG across wakeful rest during motor skill learning. During rest, participants received no cue, regular or accelerated auditory targeted-memory reactivation (TMR), or randomized tones. Neural states re-emerged in the practiced sequence order, revealing forward replay across conditions. Accelerated TMR enhanced total learning; within this condition, stronger forward replay showed the clearest exploratory relationship with micro-offline gains, while forward and reverse replay also covaried with gains across the cohort. The apparent replay timescale shifted systematically with decoder temporal resolution, showing that measured timing reflects both neural dynamics and the observation model. These findings support scalp EEG as a scalable approach for studying ordered motor-sequence reactivation during wakeful rest.

papers.title: Auditory tracking magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution during wakefulness and propofol-based anesthesia in human sEEG
papers.abstract: General anesthesia attenuates auditory responses, but response magnitude alone does not describe how residual activity aligns with sound over time or varies across the brain. We jointly characterized these aspects of auditory tracking using stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG) in 13 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy during wakefulness and clinically defined unresponsiveness under propofol-based anesthesia. The same rhythmic humming sequences were presented at approximately 1.61 Hz in both sessions. During anesthesia, stimulus-rate power showed widespread reductions and phase alignment with the stimulus rhythm was less consistent, although responses remained detectable at some recording channels. During wakefulness, response strength decreased with cortical surface distance from posteromedial Heschl's gyrus; this distance-response relationship was weaker during anesthesia. In a contrastive learning analysis (CEBRA), low-dimensional embeddings derived from anesthesia recordings yielded lower acoustic-envelope decoding accuracy on held-out data and lower consistency across model fits. Together, these findings characterize how attenuated auditory tracking is expressed jointly in response magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution.

papers.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates
papers.abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

papers.title: Daylight exposure improves sleep and subsequent sleepiness
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: The causal effects of daylight exposure on sleep remain poorly understood, particularly under real-world conditions. This study aimed to address this gap by examining the effects of an afternoon daylight intervention on subsequent sleep. Methods: Ten healthy participants (4 males; 19 to 28 years) completed two randomized 3-h afternoon outdoor walks under high-intensity light (HIL; clear goggles) or attenuated light (AL; neutral-density-filtered goggles; ~10 photopic lux) conditions. Light exposure was centered around the estimated crossover between the phase-advancing and phase-delaying portions of the light phase-response curve, individually determined from baseline dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). Subsequent nocturnal sleep was assessed using at-home polysomnography (PSG), and subjective sleepiness and sleep quality were assessed using the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and Groningen Sleep Quality Scale, respectively. Differences between conditions and across time were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Results: There were no significant differences between conditions in DLMO timing or the phase angle between DLMO and sleep onset, indicating that the light manipulation did not produce a detectable shift in circadian phase. Sleep duration and self-reported sleep quality were also unchanged. However, nighttime delta power accumulated more rapidly following HIL exposure, accompanied by greater NREM sleep and reduced wakefulness after sleep onset (all p < 0.01). Participants were also significantly less sleepy upon awakening following HIL compared with AL exposure (p < 0.05). Conclusions: High-intensity natural daylight exposure may promote greater sleep intensity and reduce sleepiness upon awakening. These findings highlight a potential role for daytime light exposure in modulating subsequent sleep physiology and next-morning sleepiness, independent of changes in circadian phase.

papers.title: Dimensionality Reduction for Cyclic Compositional Data
papers.abstract: The cyclic nature of many biological systems is frequently reflected in periodic gene expression patterns. Standard dimensionality reductions can reveal such variation but do not link a sample's position on a cycle to an ordering of the molecular features that define it. We introduce clrcycle, which applies a centered log-ratio transformation, learns a cyclic feature ordering by maximizing variance captured by the first Fourier mode, and projects samples onto the corresponding cosine and sine coordinates. The resulting two-dimensional geometry assigns each sample a phase and a radius measuring the magnitude of its projection onto the learned Fourier circle. Across a mouse circadian atlas, clrcycle recovers known temporal organization and reveals tissue-specific differences in rhythmic timing. In FUCCI-profiled single cells, clrcycle represents independently measured cell-cycle phase in two-dimensional coordinates more reliably than conventional two-dimensional embeddings. In human endometrium, a circular coordinate learned from 250 highly variable genes recovers menstrual-stage organization and can stage unseen endometrial biopsies. Together, these results establish clrcycle as powerful, explicitly circular dimensionality reduction technique to quantify high-dimensional cyclic variation across biological cycles.

papers.title: Genome-Wide Transcriptomics Uncovers a Lung-to-Aorta Inflammatory Program Driving Influenza-Induced Atherosclerosis Exacerbation
papers.abstract: Influenza infection increases cardiovascular risk in individuals with pre-existing atherosclerosis, yet the genome-wide transcriptional basis of this association remains undefined. We performed bulk RNA sequencing of aorta and lung tissues from high-fat diet-fed Apoe-/- mice infected with influenza A/PR/8/34 versus PBS-treated controls at day 15 post-infection, identifying 6,828 differentially expressed genes across both tissues (5,694 in the lung and 1,134 in the aorta; adjusted p < 0.05). In the lung, influenza sustained a CXCR3-driven chemokine storm, comprehensive Th1, Th17, and exhaustion T-cell activation programs, coordinated monocyte recruitment through Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl8, and Ccl12, a broad acute phase response including Saa3 and A2m, alveolar identity collapse through loss of Nkx2-1 and surfactant proteins, and broad metabolic dysregulation involving suppression of fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial function, and circadian metabolic regulators. In the aorta, influenza drove macrophage and DAMP activation through Trem1, Fpr2, and S100a8, cytotoxic T-cell engagement, smooth muscle cell dedifferentiation through Myocd loss, convergent bioenergetic failure, and an ectopic lung-identity gene signature representing a previously undescribed cross-organ communication mechanism. Circadian clock and Hippo/YAP pathway suppression were shared across both tissues, identifying systemic vulnerabilities connecting pulmonary infection to vascular structural compromise. Consistent with the in vivo findings, influenza-infected Apoe-/- bone marrow-derived macrophages exhibited inflammasome activation, DAMP amplification, M1 polarization, and suppression of prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory resolution. Together these findings define a lung-to-aorta inflammatory and metabolic axis driving atherosclerotic plaque destabilization during the post-infection recovery period and identify CCR2/CXCR3 antagonism, NLRP3 inhibition, and YAP pathway activation as candidate therapeutic interventions.
